f: The plan-preparation guide was updated on 13 October 2025.
The plan-preparation guide applies to England and Wales.
Deed plans are an essential element of buying and selling land.
A title plan and register cannot describe land more accurately than the pre-registration deeds allow.
Pre-registration deeds can help resolve future questions about title extent.
A lodged plan must let the land be identified clearly on the Ordnance Survey map.
A form OS2 search-of-part plan is assessed using the transfer-or-lease-of-part guidelines.
Failure to meet one guideline does not always prevent an application if the land remains identifiable.
Land that cannot be identified on the OS map may lead to rejection, requisition or cancellation.
The supplement uses one table for acceptable guidance and one for common defects.
A good plan gives buyers a clearer understanding of what they bought.
A good plan provides a sound basis if future problems arise.
A good plan helps applications be processed more efficiently and effectively.
A good plan helps reduce rejected applications.
HM Land Registry must identify both location and accurate extent relative to OS mapping.
A useful plan normally shows the extent, surrounding roads/features and relevant rights.
Unusual registration applications use the same core plan guidelines with variations.
Plans lodged with searches use the same core guidelines.
First registration requires enough detail to identify land clearly on the OS map.
A plan is necessary for most first-registration applications.
A postal description may suffice only where boundaries are clear and fully defined on OS mapping.
A verbal description is inadequate where passages, frontages, gardens or outbuildings create uncertainty.
A substituted or amended plan requested for identification must be signed by the parties.
Transfers and leases of part usually need a plan showing the transferred or leased land.
A transfer or lease plan must use the current approved estate-plan version when one exists.
A verbal description using only plot numbers or a postal address is not accepted for an approved estate plan.
A plan is required when the parent title plan has no clearly defined identifier for the part.
The seller or landlord must sign all plans forming part of the transfer or lease.
Authorised company officers may sign company transfer or lease plans.
Unusual extents can include airspace, roof-space and tunnels.
A plan is invariably required for unusual strata or similar extents.
An unusual extent must be located in relation to existing ground-surface detail.
An unusual extent application must state included or excluded depth or height.
Ordnance Survey Datum can define height to fine tolerances.
HM Land Registry may prepare a title plan instead of requisition where claimed land clearly falls outside occupied extent.
The alternative-plan route may apply where part is already registered to another owner.
The alternative-plan route may apply where part is not in the seller or landlord title.
A registration description should include postal number or house name where possible.
A registration description should include floor level where applicable.
A registration description should include road name and locality where possible.
A registration description should include town, administrative area and postcode where possible.
The plan and written property description must be accurate and must not contradict one another.
Blindly carrying forward an older description may mislead where land has been sold off.
Land should be clearly defined by edging, colouring, hatching or stippling.
An area measurement is not required for the land.
OS mapping or an approved estate layout is the most commonly acceptable base plan.
Another base may work if it is accurately drawn to scale and follows the guidance.
Hand-drawn sketches must not be used.
Architectural or engineering plans often fail because they were not prepared to define title extent.
A reduced plan can be acceptable when a bar scale is used.
Without a bar scale, a reduced plan must state that it is a reduced copy.
A reduced plan must delete the original scale endorsement when relying on recalculated scale.
A reduced plan must show its recalculated actual scale.
A PDF plan should be printed at 100 percent rather than fitted or shrunk to the page.
Preferred urban plan scales range from 1:1250 to 1:500.
The preferred rural plan scale is 1:2500.
A plan should show orientation, such as a north point.
A plan should show enough surrounding roads and features for OS-map identification.
A plan should use a metric measurement scale.
A plan should include a bar scale.
The plan should show the whole property, including associated garages, parking, bins or garden ground.
Measurements should be stated in metres to two decimal places.
Separate plans may be used to show the extent at each floor level.
Subsoil or airspace plans should show vertical levels or relate them to Ordnance Survey Datum.
Intricate internal boundaries may need a larger-scale plan such as 1:200.
An electronically lodged plan should be scanned at its original size.
An electronically lodged plan should be scanned in full colour.
Recommended scan resolution is at least 200 dpi and no more than 600 dpi.
Each scanned plan page should be no larger than A3.
A single extent should not use more than two scanned pages.
The conservation-area specification was last updated on 10 April 2026.
Ordnance Survey confirmed presumption to publish when the data meets the specification.
Conservation-area publication uses an area dataset and a document dataset.
CSV is an accepted conservation-area format.
GeoJSON is an accepted conservation-area format.
GML is an accepted conservation-area format.
GeoPackage is an accepted conservation-area format.
The data may be uploaded to a single URL.
The data may be served through an OGC WFS.
The data may be served through an ArcGIS API.
Field names may use hyphens, underscores or spaces.
Uppercase field-name characters are converted to lowercase.
A conservation area has special architectural or historic interest requiring preservation or enhancement.
Each conservation-area reference must be unique within the provider dataset.
Each conservation-area reference must remain permanent across updates.
The name field holds the official conservation-area name.
The organisation field may be blank when the local authority is responsible.
Another responsible body is identified using its organisation code.
Conservation-area geometry is a polygon or multipolygon.
WGS84 coordinates are preferred for conservation-area geometry.
Transforming non-WGS84 geometry may introduce a small precision loss.
CSV geometry is encoded as Well-Known Text.
GeoJSON, GML and GeoPackage use their associated geometry encodings.
designation-date records the official designation date.
Partial year or year-month dates are accepted when complete dates are unavailable.
document-url points to the authoritative source document, commonly a mapped PDF.
documentation-url points to a webpage introducing the document.
Each conservation area needs a unique documentation URL or anchor.
notes is optional production or interpretation text.
entry-date records when the entity was last updated.
start-date records when the record became valid, usually designation or later boundary change.
end-date records when the conservation area ceased to be valid and is blank while active.
The document dataset supplies authoritative historical and impact context.
Conservation documents may include appraisals, designation notices, management plans or gazette entries.
Each conservation document reference must be unique and permanent.
conservation-area links a document to the area reference.
The tree-preservation specification was last updated on 10 April 2026.
Ordnance Survey confirmed presumption to publish when TPO data meets the specification.
Tree-preservation publication uses order, zone and individual-tree datasets.
The tree-preservation-order dataset should be supplied as CSV.
Zone data may be CSV, GeoJSON, GML or GeoPackage.
Individual-tree data may be CSV, GeoJSON, GML or GeoPackage.
The datasets may be uploaded to one URL.
Zone and tree datasets may be served through OGC WFS.
Zone and tree datasets may be served through an ArcGIS API.
Field names may use hyphens, underscores or spaces.
Uppercase field-name characters are normalised to lowercase.
A tree preservation order protects specific trees, groups or woodlands.
The order dataset needs at least one row per order.
Each order reference must be unique within the provider dataset.
Each order reference must remain stable across updates.
An order name may use name, reference, address or be blank.
document-url points to the authoritative order or designation notice.
document-url may be cleared when an order has been revoked.
documentation-url points to a webpage introducing the order document.
Each order needs a unique documentation URL or anchor.
notes is optional production or interpretation text.
made-date records when the order became publicly available and temporary protection began.
confirmed-date records when objections were considered and full protection took effect.
entry-date records the entity's last update.
start-date records when the order came into force.
end-date records revocation and stays blank while the order is active.
A felled tree uses felled-date rather than ending the whole order.
The zone dataset needs at least one row per protected zone.
Each zone reference must be unique and permanent.
tree-preservation-order links a zone to its governing order.
Allowed zone types are area, group and woodland.
Zone geometry is a polygon or multipolygon.
All zone polygon points must use WGS84.
CSV zone geometry uses Well-Known Text.
The tree dataset needs at least one row per protected individual tree.
Each individual-tree reference must be unique and permanent.
Each tree must provide a point or polygon geometry; both may be supplied.
An individual-tree point must use WGS84.
A CSV tree point is encoded as WKT POINT.
tree-preservation-order links an individual tree to its governing order.
An individual-tree polygon or multipolygon must use WGS84.
The time-stamped DTM product is an archive of raster elevation data.
Site-specific Environment Agency LiDAR surveys have been carried out since 1998.
Some locations, including coastal areas, have been surveyed multiple times.
Time-stamped DTM data can be available at 25cm, 50cm, 1m or 2m resolution.
The time-stamped DTM is produced from the last-return LiDAR signal.
Buildings, vegetation and other surface objects are removed from the DSM.
Surface removal uses bespoke algorithms and manual editing.
Time-stamped DTM raster files are supplied as GeoTIFF.
Time-stamped DTM files are delivered in 5km zip files.
Elevation values are presented in metres.
The vertical reference is Ordnance Survey Newlyn.
The rasters are aligned to the OS National Grid.
LiDAR vertical accuracy is stated as plus or minus 15cm RMSE.
The transformation applied depends on the survey time period.
The metadata index shows which time-stamped data is available at a location.
The metadata index records specific survey dates.
The metadata index records product resolution.
The metadata index records transformation and geoidal model.
The dataset states that there are no public access constraints.
The dataset is licensed under the Open Government Licence.
The dataset metadata states a quarterly update frequency.
The coordinate reference system is EPSG:27700.
The metadata period begins on 1 December 1996.
The metadata period runs through 18 April 2024.
The Environment Agency replaced Esri image services with open WCS and WMS services.
WCS provides raw pixel elevation values rather than only a rendered image.
Updated LiDAR service endpoints remove year suffixes so future updates can remain at persistent URLs.
WCS GeoTIFF NoData pixels use the numeric sentinel -3.4028235e+38.
ArcGIS WCS does not automatically provide raster statistics and may need manual stretch settings.
ASCII grid is a generic text-based DTM format.
ASCII grid is also known as ArcInfo ASCII grid or ArcGrid ASCII.
Most standard GIS software can read the ASCII grid without translation.
The OS Terrain 50 grid download supplies ASCII data alongside GML.
The grid GML supplies location, grid spacing and vertical-reference metadata.
The grid GML supplies spatial-reference information in software-independent form.
The height data is represented as a raster grid.
Each height is calculated from the centre of a pixel.
Rows are represented from a north-west tile origin in the ASCII structure.
Each ASCII grid row reads from west to east.
Each pixel is 50 metres by 50 metres.
Each successive row begins 50 metres farther south.
A complete grid tile covers 10km by 10km.
Grid heights are supplied to the nearest 0.1 metre.
The .asc file contains the Esri ASCII grid data.
The .gml file enables the ASCII grid to be loaded as GML.
The .prj file contains the spatial reference system in Esri format.
The .asc.aux.xml file provides default styling parameters for Esri applications.
Metadata_<tile>.xml provides grid metadata such as flying date.
ContourLine, SpotHeight and LandWaterBoundary are separate GML feature types.
Contour line types include master, ordinary and auxiliary.
The master contour term corresponds to the traditional index contour.
The ordinary contour term corresponds to the traditional standard contour.
SpotHeight propertyValue stores height above Newlyn or another British height datum.
The model allows formSpot, generic, mountainPass and summit spot-height types.
The current release uses the generic spot-height subtype.
Water categories include mean high water, mean low water and Scottish spring-tide variants.
Feature identifiers use the os.t50.<tile>.<sequence> pattern.
Geometry identifiers use the feature identifier plus a .geom suffix.
Whole-tile refresh regenerates sequential feature identifiers.
OS Terrain 50 is not supplied as feature-based change-only updates.
The GML CRS is expressed as urn:ogc:def:crs:EPSG::27700.
OS Terrain 50 models ground surface after removing protruding buildings and trees.
OS Terrain 50 is an Open Data product available for commercial, educational and personal use.
The grid uses regular 50m post spacing.
Standard contour polylines use a 10m vertical interval.
OS Terrain 50 grid data is verified at 4m RMSE.
Grid creation produces no overlaps or shared edge values between tiles.
Mean high and low water breakline heights use tile-average values derived from local tide tables.
Spot heights select the highest source point inside each enclosed contour.
An interpolated spot height is not guaranteed to be the true summit.
